native_result.query: How does the effect of increasing education expenditure on per capita GDP compare between developing countries and countries in Sub-Saharan Africa?
native_result.HypoA: The effect of increasing education expenditure on per capita GDP is more pronounced in developing countries outside of Sub-Saharan Africa compared to those within it
native_result.HypoB: Increasing education expenditure is not associated with higher per-capita income in either group; where a slope is measurable it is negative in both, and it is about 6.6x steeper in raw units for the lower-middle-income ('developing') group than for Sub-Saharan Africa (-0.66 log points per +1pp of GNI, 95% CI [-1.01,-0.31], n=5, vs -0.10, 95% CI [-0.15,-0.05], n=5; raw difference -0.56, 95% CI [-0.78,-0.34], n=10) -- but that gap is a scale artefact, not a difference in sensitivity: standardised on each group's own variation the two are indistinguishable (r=-0.960 LMC vs -0.967 SSF; standardised difference +0.008, 95% CI [-0.53,+0.54], p=0.97), because SSA's education-expenditure share varied 2.9x more than LMC's in the only comparable window. This direct comparison rests on n=5 vs n=5 (2011-2015), since GNI per capita exists for Sub-Saharan Africa only from 2011. The observable channel that does differ between groups is education investment -> gross enrolment rather than -> income: SSA expanded primary gross enrolment by +36.4pp and secondary by +28.6pp over 1975-2015 while its education-expenditure share FELL 1.15pp (mean 4.30% of GNI), whereas LMC raised its share 0.37pp (mean 3.50%) for +22.7pp/+36.7pp of enrolment; in differenced terms a +1pp rise in the share predicts no enrolment gain in either group (LMC -0.78pp primary, 95% CI [-2.28,+0.71], p=0.30, n=40, and -0.79pp secondary, [-1.71,+0.14], p=0.09; SSF +0.25pp primary, [-1.27,+1.77], p=0.74, and -0.26pp secondary, [-0.91,+0.38], p=0.41; group contrasts p=0.34 and p=0.52, n=80). On the income side the association is fragile and specification-driven for the comparison group (LMC growth on lagged expenditure -0.023 [-0.064,+0.018] p=0.27 n=40 without exports and -0.028 [-0.068,+0.013] p=0.18 with exports; +0.002 [-0.029,+0.032] p=0.91 in a dynamic AR(1) spec; +0.030 [-0.054,+0.113] p=0.47 once labour force participation is added on the shorter 1991-2015 sample; only the enrolment-controlled spec reaches -0.048, p=0.010, which over-controls the total effect), and Sub-Saharan Africa's income series supports no growth equation at all (4 usable observations). Levels elasticities (LMC -0.67 [-1.10,-0.24]; SSF -0.25 [-1.39,+0.89]) are trend-driven descriptive colour: lag-1 autocorrelations are ~1 in levels and the levels correlations collapse or flip sign on differencing (LMC education-expenditure vs GNIpc -0.48 -> +0.08; primary enrolment vs GNIpc +0.91 -> -0.01). Per-capita GDP is measured by GNI per capita in constant 2015 US$ because no GDP-per-capita series exists in these data; 'developing countries' means the Lower middle income (LMC) aggregate; education expenditure is 'Adjusted savings: education expenditure (% of GNI)', not the % of total government expenditure named in the dataset description, which is absent; both series are pre-aggregated groups (N=2 units), so fixed-effects or dynamic-panel estimators are inestimable; and because the expenditure measure is a share of GNI, income shocks move the regressor mechanically while incomes rose (LMC +3.2%/yr, SSA +1.2%/yr) and education shares fell in the 2011-2015 window. This is an association, not a causal effect.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Wide->long reshape via regex on the 41 '1975 [YR1975]' header columns, to_numeric(errors=coerce), tidy 492-row long panel -> 82-row group x year panel; coverage documented (SSF GNIpc 5 obs, LFPR and SSF exports from 1991, 84/492 blanks, zero non-numeric junk); no imputation and no external data. 2) Spuriousness diagnostics: coverage, lag-1 autocorrelation in levels vs first differences, and levels vs first-difference vs detrended correlations. 3) Primary evidence: differenced and lagged education-expenditure -> primary/secondary gross enrolment, per group and pooled with group interaction (1975-2015), in raw units and within-group z-scored. 4) Direct-literal: matched-window 2011-2015 log-GNIpc slopes per group, pooled group interaction, within-window standardised version, growth version, and Pearson r with Bartlett effective-sample-size inflated CIs. 5) LMC growth equations with/without exports growth, with/without labour force participation, dynamic AR(1), and 5-year non-overlapping long differences; SSA growth equation reported only to show non-estimability. 6) Levels log-log elasticities computed and explicitly labelled trend-driven colour. 7) SE hygiene: Newey-West(4) only when n>=20; whenever HAC gave narrower intervals than classical OLS the wider classical interval was reported and flagged in se_type; models with residual df<8 auto-labelled DESCRIPTIVE ONLY. 8) Every coefficient cited in the hypothesis was programmatically matched against results_summary.csv (18/18 exact) and key slopes re-derived with hand-written normal-equation OLS.

sub_hypo.text: The effect of increasing education expenditure on per capita GDP is more pronounced in developing countries outside of Sub-Saharan Africa compared to those within it.

sub_hypo.text: Higher education-expenditure shares are negatively associated with log per-capita income in both groups in the comparable window; the raw slope is about 6.6 times steeper in LMC.

sub_hypo.text: Year-to-year increases in education-expenditure share predict no statistically supported enrolment gain in either group, and the groups' differenced associations do not significantly differ.
